cues.s: Follow one token through a frontier model.
The token is "sat", with its leading space, in the sentence: the cat sat on the mat.
The model is DeepSeek V4 Pro, whose design is published.
Chapter one: data and tokens.
Web pages, code, books, math and synthetic reasoning traces are pooled into a single stream, thirty-three trillion tokens of it.
Copies are hashed and removed, so nothing is learned twice.
Filters drop low-quality text and personal data, and the mix is rebalanced so no source dominates.
The tokenizer cuts text into pieces from a fixed vocabulary.
Common words become one token, and the leading space travels with the word.
So our token is "sat", space included.
Rare words split into several pieces, each an integer ID, from a vocabulary of one hundred twenty-nine thousand, two hundred and eighty.
Images take another road: their patches become vectors, not IDs.
Chapter two: pretraining.
Batches of sequences flow up through every layer at once, and a causal mask makes sure no position can peek at the future.

clips.title: Score the guess, send gradients down

cues.s: After "the cat", the model spreads probability over the whole vocabulary.
The loss measures how surprised it was by "sat".
Gradients flow back down, and every weight takes a small step.

clips.title: Sharded across racks, trained in FP8

cues.s: The one point six trillion parameter model is split across racks of accelerators, using several kinds of parallelism at once.
It trains in eight-bit precision, and the released model stores its experts in four bits.
Then the memory stretches.
Pretraining lengthens the context in stages, from four thousand tokens to sixteen thousand, then sixty-four thousand, and finally one million.
Chapter three: post-training.
First, separate specialists for math, code, agents and instructions are trained on worked examples, and then with reinforcement learning.
For a prompt with a checkable answer, the policy, which is the same tower, samples a group of attempts.
The group of eight in the drawing is illustrative.
Verifiers grade code and math, and rubrics grade open-ended answers.
Each score is compared with the group's average, so no separate value model is needed.
Winning attempts are reinforced, with a penalty that keeps each specialist close to where it started.
Then distillation merges all the specialists into one model.
Chapter four: inside the model.
The token ID picks one row of the embedding table, a lookup, not a calculation.
Out comes a vector of seven thousand, one hundred and sixty-eight numbers.
A normalized copy of the vector goes into attention.
"Sat" can score every earlier token, while a causal mask hides the ones that come later.
To reach a million tokens, attention compresses its memory.
Some layers read a sparse selection of compressed blocks plus a recent window.
Others read heavily compressed summaries.
Attention's output is added back to the residual stream, which here runs as four parallel lanes, mixed by learned connections that keep the signal stable through the depth of the tower.
A router scores three hundred and eighty-four experts and keeps the top six, while one shared expert always runs.
That is why only forty-nine billion of the one point six trillion parameters work on each token.
The block repeats sixty-one times, each layer with its own weights: a stack, not a loop.
The first three layers route tokens by hash instead of a learned router.
At the top, a final norm and the output head turn the vector into one score for every token in the vocabulary.
A second head guesses one token further ahead.

clips.title: Training: loss up top, gradients down

cues.s: In training, the top score is compared with the real next token, "on".
The loss flows back down as gradients.
There is no K V cache, because the whole sequence runs at once.
In serving, the same tower is frozen, and the pass only goes up.
Each attention layer writes its compressed memory into the K V cache, and the top output goes to a sampler.
Chapter five: serving your request.
The gateway checks your key, your rate limits and your reasoning setting, screens for abuse, and routes you to a warm replica.
Modern engines split the work.
One pool of accelerators reads prompts and another writes replies, and requests join the batch at every step instead of waiting their turn.

clips.title: Prefill: read it all at once

cues.s: Prefill reads your whole prompt in one parallel pass.
It is compute-bound, it fills the K V cache, "sat" included, and it sets the time to the first token.
Decode writes one token per step: first hidden reasoning, then the reply.
Each step streams the weights and the cache through memory, so it is memory-bound.
Drafting a few tokens ahead speeds it up.
The sampler picks the next token, and keeps tool calls in valid JSON.
Text is decoded into a buffer, checked by output guardrails, and only then streamed to you.

clips.title: The model stops with a tool call

cues.s: Chapter six: the tool loop.
Instead of more text, the model can stop with a tool call, a name and its arguments, and hand control back to your app.

clips.title: Your app or an MCP server runs it

cues.s: Your app, or an M C P server, runs the tool and keeps the result.
Treat that result as untrusted input: it is where prompt injection usually arrives.
The API remembers nothing between calls, so your app sends the whole conversation again, with the tool call and its result appended.

clips.title: Prefix cache: prefill only what's new

cues.s: The server recognizes the unchanged prefix, "sat" included, and reuses its cached memory.
Only the new tokens are read, and decoding continues to the final answer.
Thirty stops, one token.
From a page of training text to the answer on your screen, it is the same tower, used two ways.
